To exploit one, two requests must start being processed within that millisecond. The obstacle is **network jitter**: the variation in how long packets take to cross the network, caused by queues in routers and the operating systems on both ends. Two requests sent at the same instant from far away can arrive several milliseconds apart, so a 1 ms window is mostly missed.

**Last-byte sync** was the older answer, for HTTP/1.1. A server only starts processing a request once it has the whole request. So the tester opens several connections, sends each request except its final byte, waits, then sends all the final bytes together. Most of each request has already arrived; only the tiny final pieces have to race. Kettle implemented this in **Turbo Intruder**, an open-source extension for Burp Suite (an add-on scripted in Python for sending large or precisely timed batches of requests). It helps, but the final bytes still travel in separate packets, each with its own jitter.

**The single-packet attack**, which Kettle presented at the Black Hat USA security conference in 2023 in the paper "Smashing the state machine", removes network jitter instead of reducing it. It relies on **HTTP/2** (RFC 9113), the version of HTTP that carries many requests over one TCP connection at once. Each request is a **stream** made of **frames**, and the last frame of a request carries an `END_STREAM` flag, which "indicates that this frame is the last that the endpoint will send for the identified stream".

The idea: send the bulk of 20 to 30 requests on one connection, withhold the final frame of each, then send all the withheld frames together so they arrive **in one TCP packet**. One packet cannot be split by jitter, so every request becomes complete at the same instant. Kettle used **Nagle's algorithm** (RFC 896, 1984, by John Nagle, then at Ford Aerospace: a TCP rule that holds back small writes while earlier data is unacknowledged, which batches them) to get those final frames into one packet. The approach was inspired by the 2020 USENIX Security paper (USENIX, a computing systems association, runs the USENIX Security Symposium) [Timeless Timing Attacks](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity20/presentation/van-goethem) by Tom Van Goethem, Christina Pöpper, Wouter Joosen and Mathy Vanhoef, which put two whole HTTP/2 requests in one packet to compare server processing times.

blocks.title: Kettle's benchmark: 20 requests, Melbourne to Dublin (17,000 km)

scenes.caption: Last-byte sync: the gap between the first and last request starting to execute had a median of 4 ms and a standard deviation of 3 ms. A 1 ms window is usually missed.
Single-packet attack: median spread 1 ms, standard deviation 0.3 ms. Kettle calls it 4 to 10 times more effective by these measures.
On one real vulnerability, the single-packet attack succeeded after about 30 seconds, where last-byte sync took over two hours.

blocks.md: Why a smaller spread matters so much, in a simplified model. Suppose two requests start processing at independent, uniformly random moments within a spread of $s$ milliseconds, and they collide if their start times are less than the window $w$ apart. The chance of a collision is:

blocks.caption: Simplified: real arrival times are not uniform, and one attempt can carry 20 to 30 requests, which raises the odds further.

blocks.title: Chance two requests hit a window of w ms, by arrival spread

scenes.caption: Window 1 ms. With last-byte sync's median spread of 4 ms, a pair collides about 44% of the time; at the single-packet median of 1 ms, every time.
A tighter window of 0.5 ms: about 23% at 4 ms of spread, 75% at 1 ms. Shrinking the spread matters more than shrinking the window.
A sloppy endpoint with a 5 ms window collides every time at both marked spreads (1 and 4 ms), and still 44% of the time at 20 ms. Slow code is the easiest to race, whatever the network.

blocks.md: **Tools, and what they show.** Burp Suite 2023.9 added sending a **group of requests in parallel** to Burp Repeater (Burp's tool for editing and resending requests): it uses last-byte sync for HTTP/1 and the single-packet technique for HTTP/2. Turbo Intruder offers the same with scripting. Their output is a set of responses with timings; the tell-tale result is a mix that should be impossible when the same requests are sent one by one (five "applied" for a one-time code). Use them only on your own systems, on systems you have written permission to test, or in PortSwigger's free race condition labs, which were built so that the windows are realistic.

**Defender view.** *What it looks like*: a burst of 20 to 30 requests to one endpoint on a single HTTP/2 connection, all starting within about a millisecond, often with identical bodies. That is visible in server logs that record connection ids and request start times with millisecond precision. *What it means*: you cannot rely on timing to protect a check-then-act. The OWASP cheat sheet's rule is "If the window exists at all, assume it's exploitable". Turning off HTTP/2 is not a fix either: it removes the best tool, not the bug, and last-byte sync still works over HTTP/1.1. *Prevent*: the atomic patterns of lesson 9. *Detect*: the burst shape above, plus any one-time action that succeeded twice.

The single-packet attack made network distance irrelevant: a tester far away can now hit a 1 ms window about as reliably as one on the same network. Treat every check-then-act as reachable, and fix it with atomicity, not with speed.

blocks.question: Why does putting the final frames of 20 HTTP/2 requests into one TCP packet defeat network jitter?
options: Because HTTP/2 encrypts the frames
Because TCP packets travel faster than HTTP/1.1 packets
Because a single packet arrives as a unit, so all 20 requests become complete at the same instant regardless of the path's delay variation
Because the server processes HTTP/2 requests in a single thread
blocks.explain: Jitter changes when each packet arrives. If the bytes that complete every request are in one packet, they all arrive together, so the server sees 20 complete requests at once. Encryption and speed are irrelevant, and HTTP/2 servers still process streams concurrently.

blocks.question: A team says: "our race window is under a millisecond, so we will fix it later". Using the simplified model, what is the best reply?
options: Disagree: with a 1 ms arrival spread a pair of requests hits a 1 ms window every time, and one attempt can carry 20 to 30 requests
Agreed, a 1 ms window cannot be hit remotely
Agreed, as long as HTTP/2 is disabled
Disagree, because the model says windows below 1 ms are always hit by last-byte sync
blocks.explain: In the model, P = 1 when the spread is no larger than the window, and the single-packet attack's median spread was 1 ms. Disabling HTTP/2 leaves last-byte sync, and last-byte sync's 4 ms median spread still gives about 44% per pair.

lessons.title: Hidden sub-states: Kettle's GitLab email race (CVE-2022-4037)

blocks.md:
Limit overruns are the obvious races. Kettle's 2023 research started from one that was not. In 2016 Josip Franjković, a security researcher, wrote of having "somehow succeeded to confirm a random email address" on Facebook, and neither Franjković nor Facebook could explain it for two months: changing an account's email to two different addresses at the same moment could produce one email carrying two confirmation codes. Seven years later Kettle set out to understand it.

Kettle's summary: "with race conditions, everything is multi-step". A single HTTP request may move the application through several short-lived **sub-states** (the term from lesson 6) before it finishes. If a second request touches the same data while the first is in one of them, the result can be a state no designer drew: not "one too many" but "the wrong thing entirely". The methodology targets these collisions, and the paper's case studies were mostly about email, because email verification is a security decision many sites trust.

**GitLab, the first clue.** GitLab (a code hosting and build platform) lets you invite people to a project by email. Kettle sent six identical invitation requests. One after another: six success responses and one email. All at once with the single-packet attack: one success, five "The member's email address has already been taken", and **two emails**. Two emails from requests that mostly failed meant a hidden sub-state. On its own that gave only a low-severity bug (a dummy invitation masking an admin one), but it pointed at deeper problems.

**The real bug.** Changing the account email took 220 ms, fast for an operation that sends mail, which hinted the mail was sent from another thread. So Kettle asked GitLab to change the address to two different addresses at the same moment. Sometimes the message sent to one address contained the confirmation link for the other, and the token in it was often valid. By pairing Kettle's own address with `albinowaxed@gitlab.com`, Kettle received a working link for the GitLab address and ended up with it as a **verified** email on the profile.

blocks.title: Two email changes, one misrouted token (simplified model)

scenes.caption: Request 1 changes the email to the tester's own address. The handler stores it as unconfirmed with token t1 and queues a mail to that address.
Request 2, in the race window, changes the same account's email to the target address. It overwrites the stored address and token.
The mail worker builds the first message. The recipient came with the job, but the body is rendered from the database, which now holds the target address and t2.
The tester receives a link that confirms admin@victim.test with a valid token. Clicking it marks an address they do not own as verified.

blocks.md: **Why a verified email matters.** On GitLab, a verified address can claim pending project invitations sent to it. And GitLab acts as an identity provider for other sites (its users can sign in elsewhere with their GitLab account), so any site that trusts GitLab's word that an address is verified could be taken over. The NVD (National Vulnerability Database) entry for **CVE-2022-4037** says it plainly: "A race condition can lead to verified email forgery and takeover of third-party accounts when using GitLab as an OAuth provider" (OAuth is the standard protocol behaviour behind "sign in with" buttons), affecting GitLab's Community and Enterprise Editions before 15.5.7, 15.6 before 15.6.4 and 15.7 before 15.7.2 (fixed in 15.7.2 on 4 January 2023, per Kettle), classed as CWE-362. GitLab rated it medium (6.4 on CVSS 3.1, the Common Vulnerability Scoring System), while NVD's own score is 8.5 (high); Kettle wrote that they would rate it high because of the invitation hijack.

**The root cause was in Devise**, a widely used authentication library for Ruby on Rails, a Ruby web framework (NCC Group, a security consultancy, called it "far and away the most popular authentication system for Rails"). Devise passed the recipient address to the mailer as an argument, but the email body, including the confirmation link, was rendered later by a template that read the token and unconfirmed address back from the database. Between those two moments, another request could change the database. Kettle tried for 200 days to report it to Devise through three security contacts without success. Devise finally fixed it in version 5.0.3 in March 2026 ([GHSA-57hq-95w6-v4fc](https://github.com/heartcombo/devise/security/advisories/GHSA-57hq-95w6-v4fc), CVE-2026-32700), crediting Kettle as a reporter: upgrade any Devise app.

blocks.code:
# Simplified model of the GitLab/Devise email race (not their real code)
from itertools import count
tokens = (f"t{n}" for n in count(1))
db = {"unconfirmed": None, "token": None}
queue, outbox = [], []

def change_email(new):                  # web request handler
    db["unconfirmed"] = new
    db["token"] = next(tokens)
    queue.append(new)                   # recipient: from the argument

def mail_worker():                      # runs later, on another thread
    to = queue.pop(0)                   # body: read back from the database
    outbox.append(f"to {to}: confirm {db['unconfirmed']} with {db['token']}")

change_email("me@attacker.test")        # request 1
change_email("admin@victim.test")       # request 2 lands in the race window
mail_worker(); mail_worker()
print(*outbox, sep="\n")
print("valid token:", db["token"], "for", db["unconfirmed"])
blocks.caption: A simplified model of the bug: the recipient travels with the job, the body is read back from shared state later.

blocks.code:
to me@attacker.test: confirm admin@victim.test with t2
to admin@victim.test: confirm admin@victim.test with t2
valid token: t2 for admin@victim.test
blocks.caption: Real output. The first message goes to the attacker but carries the victim address's valid token. Simplified: the real exploit also needed Devise's resend-existing-token path.

from itertools import count
tokens = (f"t{n}" for n in count(1))
db = {"unconfirmed": None, "token": None}
queue, outbox = [], []

def change_email(new):
    token = next(tokens)
    db["unconfirmed"], db["token"] = new, token
    queue.append((new, token))          # address and token travel together

def mail_worker():
    to, token = queue.pop(0)
    outbox.append(f"to {to}: confirm {to} with {token}")

change_email("me@attacker.test")
change_email("admin@victim.test")
mail_worker(); mail_worker()
print(*outbox, sep="\n")
print("valid token:", db["token"], "for", db["unconfirmed"])
blocks.caption: The fix in the model: the address and the token are decided once and travel together in the job.

blocks.code:
to me@attacker.test: confirm me@attacker.test with t1
to admin@victim.test: confirm admin@victim.test with t2
valid token: t2 for admin@victim.test
blocks.caption: Real output. Each recipient gets a token for their own address only, so t2 never reaches the attacker.

blocks.md:
**Other sub-state families** from Kettle's paper, in one line each:

- **Multi-endpoint**: an order request validates payment and then confirms; a parallel add-to-cart lands between the two, so an item is confirmed but never paid for (lesson 4's workflow bug, inside one request).
- **Session-based**: a password reset that stores the username and token in the session; two parallel resets in one session for two usernames can leave the session holding the victim's username with a token that was emailed to the attacker.
- **Partial construction**: a user row is inserted and its password set by a second statement; in between the password is null, and an input that matches that empty value may be accepted.
- **Deferred**: batch jobs that run later create the collision themselves; Kettle found one where the two conflicting email changes could be 20 minutes apart.

Testers should know that the default session handler of PHP (a server-side web language) runs one request per session at a time, which can hide a race that two sessions expose (Homakov's two browsers).

**Defences, from Kettle's paper**: avoid mixing data from different sources (Devise read the token from the database but the address from an argument; one source would have been safe); make sensitive state changes atomic using the datastore's concurrency features; use uniqueness constraints as defence in depth; never use one storage layer to secure another; keep sessions internally consistent (write a request's session changes as one batch, not variable by variable); and remember that an ORM which hides transactions is responsible for them. Some designs avoid server-side state by keeping it client-side in a signed token, which has its own risks.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: the defences above, and treat "verified" flags as security decisions: set them only from a token that was generated for, stored with and sent to the same address. *Detect*: several email-change or reset requests for one account within milliseconds; mail jobs whose recipient differs from the address named in the message (log both). *Respond*: revoke verifications completed in a suspicious window, re-verify affected addresses, and tell relying sites that trust your verified emails.

Every request is a sequence of steps, so every endpoint that edits shared state has sub-states. Decide each security-relevant value once, carry it with the work, and make the state change atomic, rather than writing a value early and reading it back later.

blocks.question: In the Devise bug, which change removes the race window without adding any lock?
options: Sending the email before saving the token
Passing the token and the address together to the mailer, so the body never reads shared state that another request can change
Making the token longer
Rendering the email in the same thread as the request
blocks.explain: The window existed because the recipient and the body came from different sources at different times. Deciding both once and passing them together means a concurrent change cannot mix them. A longer token does not help; same-thread rendering narrows the window but the body would still read back from the database.

blocks.question: Kettle's GitLab invitation probe returned one success, five "already taken" errors and two emails when sent in parallel, but six successes and one email when sent one by one. What does this tell a tester?
options: Nothing, error responses under load are normal
The server is rate limiting the tester
The deviation from the sequential baseline is a clue to a hidden sub-state worth investigating, even though no exploit is visible yet
Invitations are processed by PHP's session lock
blocks.explain: Kettle's method is to benchmark sequential behaviour first and treat any deviation under parallel load (different responses, extra emails, odd timing) as a clue. Two emails from mostly failed requests means some step ran twice. Without the baseline, the five errors would have looked normal.

lessons.title: Testing logic: invariants, abuse cases and concurrency tests

blocks.md:
Logic flaws survive ordinary tests because ordinary tests check that the feature works: add an item, pay, receive the order. Nobody tests that the feature cannot be bent. The OWASP cheat sheet proposes **the dishonest user exercise**: sit with the specification and "imagine a user whose only goal is to extract maximum value while staying within the letter of the system's rules". That user sends no malicious payloads; they use the app "exactly as designed, just in an order or volume the designer didn't anticipate".

Its questions to ask early, for every feature: Can the user skip a step, repeat one, or do them out of order? Can two users act on the same object at the same time? Can one user act from two directions at once (two tabs, two devices)? What does this feature produce that has value? And for each invariant: what enforces it, and "is that enforcement atomic?"

**Abuse cases** turn those answers into backlog items. An abuse case (a close cousin of the misuse case) describes how a feature could be used against its owner, written next to the normal user stories so it gets estimated, built and tested. The OWASP Abuse Case Cheat Sheet describes a workshop process for this, though OWASP has since archived it, noting that reviewers found abuse cases "rarely used in practice" and the framework heavyweight. A lighter version works well for logic: for each invariant, write one abuse case and one test.

- Invariant: a coupon is used at most once per user. Abuse case: redeem it from 20 parallel requests. Test: race 20 redemptions, expect exactly one success.
- Invariant: an order ships only what was paid for. Abuse case: add an item after payment. Test: pay, add, confirm, expect 409.
- Invariant: refunds never exceed the captured amount. Abuse case: two partial refunds, sequential and parallel. Test: both orders of events.

blocks.title: Which kind of test can reveal which broken invariant (1 = can)

scenes.caption: Rows are invariants from this course; columns are kinds of test. A 1 means that test can expose a violation of that invariant.
One-by-one tests catch simple reuse and stale rules, but never a race: in sequence, check-then-act code behaves correctly.
Edited values (negative, huge, missing) and skipped or reordered steps catch lessons 2 and 4. Each covers only part of the table.
Only the parallel column covers every row: each invariant here is a check-then-act somewhere, so each needs at least one concurrency test.

blocks.md: **Manual testing, in the OWASP and PortSwigger checklists.** The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide has a business logic chapter whose tests include Test Business Logic Data Validation, Test Ability to Forge Requests, Test Integrity Checks, Test for Process Timing, Test Number of Times a Function Can Be Used Limits (WSTG-BUSL-05) and Testing for the Circumvention of Work Flows (WSTG-BUSL-06). PortSwigger's practical advice for each request: remove each parameter in turn (both the value and the whole parameter, one at a time), try values far outside the normal range and of the wrong type, and follow multi-step processes to the end to see what a change in one step does later. For workflows, use forced browsing: skip steps, repeat them, go back, and send a later step first.

**Testing for races**, on systems you are authorised to test. Kettle's method has three steps:

1. **Predict collisions.** Pick security-critical objects (users, sessions, orders, balances) and the endpoints that write them. A collision needs two operations on the *same record*: a reset token stored per user id cannot collide across two users, but one stored in the session can.
2. **Probe for clues.** First record a **baseline** by sending a group of requests one by one; then send the same group in parallel (single-packet attack, or last-byte sync over HTTP/1.1) and look for any deviation: different responses, extra or odd emails, unexpected timing. Kettle regards "spotting anomalies as the single most important skill for finding race conditions".
3. **Prove the concept.** Understand what happened, cut down to the fewest requests (usually two), and repeat until it is reliable, then report.

Kettle also warns that, in their experience, race conditions are "extremely challenging" to identify through pure code analysis alone, so black-box testing is worth doing even with the source.

For developers, the strongest test is an automated one that races the real code against a real database on every build. The cheat sheet: "If two requests can race, write a test that races them", and assert the end state ("balance is never negative, coupon is redeemed exactly once"). This pytest test releases 20 connections at once through a barrier and states the invariant as two assertions. It runs against both lesson 9 functions.

blocks.code:
import threading, psycopg, pytest
from common import DSN, reset
from vuln import read_then_debit
from fix_a import conditional_update

@pytest.mark.parametrize("withdraw", [read_then_debit, conditional_update])
def test_balance_never_overdrawn(withdraw):
    reset()                                   # one account holding 100
    n = 20
    conns = [psycopg.connect(DSN, autocommit=True) for _ in range(n)]
    gate, results = threading.Barrier(n), []
    def worker(c):
        gate.wait()                           # release all 20 together
        results.append(withdraw(c))
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(c,)) for c in conns]
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()
    with psycopg.connect(DSN) as c:
        balance = c.execute("SELECT balance FROM accounts").fetchone()[0]
    assert results.count("paid") == 1         # the invariant, as a test
    assert balance == 0
blocks.caption: A concurrency test in pytest (a Python test framework), parametrised over the vulnerable and fixed withdrawal from lesson 9.

blocks.md: Write the invariant first, then a test that tries to break it in every way this course showed: odd values, odd order, and many at once. A test suite with no parallel test cannot fail on a race.

A concurrency test that passes once proves little: races are probabilistic. Use many parallel workers, a barrier so they start together, a real database rather than a mock, and run it on every build so a later refactor that reopens the window is caught.

blocks.question: A team's test applies a coupon twice in a row and checks the second is refused. Which bug can this test never find?
options: A coupon redeemed twice by two requests that arrive at the same moment
A coupon accepted after its expiry date
A coupon applied to a product it was not meant for
A coupon code that is case-insensitive
blocks.explain: Sequentially, the second request always sees the first redemption, so check-then-act code passes. Only a test that sends the redemptions concurrently can reveal the race. The other bugs are visible one request at a time.

blocks.question: In Kettle's predict step, why is a password reset that stores the token in the users table (keyed by user id) a poor race target, while one that stores it in the session is a good one?
options: Session storage is always slower
Users tables cannot be locked
Session tokens are shorter
Two resets for two different users write two different rows, so they never collide; two resets in one session write the same session record
blocks.explain: A collision needs two operations on the same record. Keyed by user id, parallel resets for two users touch two rows. Keyed by session, both requests overwrite the same session's username and token, which can leave them mismatched.

lessons.title: Detecting and responding to logic and race abuse

blocks.md:
Even a well-designed feature will meet a creative abuser, and many logic flaws are found in production first. Detection for this bug class looks different from detection for injection: there is no malicious payload to match, only **legitimate requests in an impossible pattern** and **books that do not add up**.

The OWASP cheat sheet's **what to log**, for every operation that dispenses value, changes permissions or moves money: the authenticated user, the target resource, the action, the outcome, request context to reconstruct it (IP, user agent, correlation ID), and business context to audit it (the price computed, the coupon applied, the new state). It adds that these logs "should be tamper-evident and separate from general application logs".

**What to alert on**, from the same cheat sheet: sign-ups from one IP, device fingerprint or payment instrument; repeated failed password resets from one source; unusually high rates of promo redemptions, referral completions or credit issuance; bursts of requests to one endpoint from one user; and workflows that "complete in substantially less time than a human would need". Its advice: "You don't need sophisticated machine learning for this. Simple thresholds on per-user, per-IP, and per-device rates catch most automated abuse."

For automated abuse of business flows (lesson 3), the OWASP API Security Top 10's API6 lists device fingerprinting, human detection (CAPTCHA or behavioural signals), non-human patterns such as adding to cart and completing the purchase in under a second, and considering blocks on Tor exit nodes (where traffic from the Tor anonymity network leaves it) and known proxies.

blocks.caption: A burst rule over the value-event log: the same user hitting the same endpoint at least 3 times within 10 ms.

blocks.code: ALERT u7 POST /coupon: 4 requests within 10 ms, 3 succeeded
blocks.caption: Real output. u9's two redemptions, 3.9 s apart, and u3's transfers do not fire. Three successes on a one-time coupon is a confirmed race, not just a suspicious burst.

blocks.md: Bursts catch an attack while it happens. **Reconciliation** catches what bursts miss, including lost updates that leave a plausible balance. The idea: keep an append-only **ledger** (one row per credit or debit) next to each balance, and regularly check the invariant that each balance equals the sum of its ledger entries. Other useful invariant queries: one-time grants per user (`GROUP BY user_id, code HAVING count(*) > 1`), refunds above captured amounts, negative balances, and total customer balances against the funds actually held (Flexcoin's hot wallet).

blocks.caption: Reconciliation in SQL: balances that disagree with their ledgers.

Real output from psql, PostgreSQL's command-line client (PostgreSQL 17). Wallet 1 looks fine at 0, but its ledger records five payouts from a 100 deposit: the lost update from lessons 5 and 9, found after the fact.

blocks.title: From signal to fix: the response loop for logic abuse

nodes.label:
Contain: flag off,
freeze, halt payouts

scenes.caption: Two detection paths feed one queue: real-time burst rules over the value-event log, and scheduled invariant queries over the ledger.

Contain first: switch the endpoint off with a feature flag (a switch that turns code on or off without a deploy) or freeze the affected codes, cards or accounts, and halt withdrawals or shipping, the step that turns a bad number into a real loss.
Scope and recover: query the logs and ledger for every account that used the flaw, then void orders, reverse credits and claw back value.
Fix and verify: make the check atomic (lesson 9), then re-test with parallel requests. Kettle saw two companies' first fixes fail under retest.
Close the loop: add the concurrency test to the build and a detection rule for the pattern. "A detection that doesn't lead to a prevention is a detection you'll be making again next month."

blocks.md:
**Responding.** The order matters: contain, scope, recover, fix, verify, prevent. Kettle's warning about fixes deserves its own line: after Kettle's deferred-collision report, "the initial fix attempt made the misrouted token invalid most of the time, but not always", and another company's first fix was also incomplete, so "race condition patches definitely deserve scrutiny". Retest every fix with the same parallel method that found the bug, not with a single request.

Finally, handle reporters well. Homakov needed five weeks to reach anyone at Starbucks and then got a call about fraud. A published security contact and a disclosure policy (the security basics course covered disclosure) make the next report arrive sooner and kinder.

Log every value-changing event with business context, alert on impossible patterns (one-time actions that succeed twice, bursts within milliseconds, flows faster than a human), and reconcile balances against ledgers. Then contain before you investigate, and retest fixes in parallel.

**Practise legally.** Work only on systems you own or are authorised to test.

- PortSwigger's free Web Security Academy has interactive labs for [business logic vulnerabilities](https://portswigger.net/web-security/logic-flaws) (including the excessive trust, negative quantity, integer overflow and workflow labs this course described) and [race conditions](https://portswigger.net/web-security/all-labs#race-conditions) (limit overrun, multi-endpoint, single-endpoint and partial construction labs, built with realistic windows).
- OWASP Juice Shop, a deliberately insecure web shop you run yourself, has a race challenge, "Multiple Likes" (like one review three times as one user), described in its [Broken Anti Automation](https://pwning.owasp-juice.shop/companion-guide/latest/part2/broken-anti-automation.html) chapter.
- Run this course's lesson 9 scripts against your own local PostgreSQL, break them, and then write the concurrency test that catches each break.

blocks.question: A wallet balance reads 0 and no alert fired, but its ledger sums to -400. Which detection caught the problem, and what kind of race left it?
options: A burst rule; a limit overrun with a negative balance
A web application firewall (WAF) signature; SQL injection
Reconciliation of balance against ledger; a lost update, where later writes overwrote earlier ones
A rate limit; credential stuffing
blocks.explain: The balance itself looks valid, so only comparing it with the ledger reveals the gap. A lost update (writing a value computed from a stale read) produces exactly this: five recorded payouts, one visible debit.

blocks.question: A team fixes a coupon race and verifies the fix by applying the coupon twice in a row. What should they do instead?
options: Nothing more, two sequential attempts prove the fix
Retest with many parallel requests, ideally the same method that found the bug, and add a concurrency test to the build
Ask the reporter to stop testing
Add a CAPTCHA and close the ticket
blocks.explain: A sequential retest passes even on vulnerable code. Kettle saw incomplete race fixes at two companies; only a parallel retest shows whether the window is closed, and a concurrency test keeps it closed.
